turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Thursday, the twentieth of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go. [excited] Claire, what's on the front?
Three things. A ghost-fleet tanker no one will claim, fouling a coast that joined no war. The Gulf's worst slick in years.
A dinosaur dropped into a suburban cul-de-sac — and the critics liking it more than the crowd did.
And a whole hobby built on breaking watches open on purpose, where the tools cost more than the watch. There's a thread running through all of it.
[curious] Which is?
The middleman, getting routed around. Every desk today, someone decides the go-between isn't worth it anymore. Hold that. Start with the ship.
Okay. Off southern Oman. Walk me through it.
[thoughtful] A tanker called the Caroline Bezengi. Cameroon flag, eight hundred thousand barrels of Russian crude aboard. Part of the shadow fleet Moscow uses to move oil around the price cap.
Its crew reported a suspected explosion on the eighth of June. Nobody has claimed it — no country, no group.
[thoughtful] And then it's just left there?
Three weeks later it ran aground inside a protected Omani marine reserve. And it sat, leaking, through a whole monsoon that pushed the oil the wrong way.
So the oil reaches the coast.

By the eighteenth, more than two thousand square kilometres of the Arabian Sea. Beaches near Ras Madrakah, blackened. About forty kilometres of shoreline expected to be hit. This is a sanctioned dark-fleet vessel, under both British and European sanctions, and the country paying for it is a bystander.
Reef, seagrass, endangered-turtle nesting sand, and the feeding grounds of the Arabian Sea humpback whale. The resort island of Masirah is next in the oil's path.
[sighs] And Oman put not a single barrel of that anywhere.
That's the whole point. It joined no war. It moved no cargo. It just happened to be downwind.
Now — you said the cleanup stalled for a strange reason.
The tanker's insurer is itself a sanctioned Russian firm. So salvage could only be funded once Western authorities granted waivers to be paid.
[scoffs] So the machinery built to squeeze Moscow ended up squeezing the cleanup.
Lloyd's List called it, and I'm quoting — the spill that sanctions built.
How do the different desks frame it?
Kyiv reads it as made in Moscow — a fleet of ageing, opaquely-insured tankers now spilling disasters far from the front line.
Doha keeps the coast in the frame: a non-belligerent nation left holding the ecological bill, while the numbers are still disputed.
And our sceptic?
[skeptical] That dispute is the story. Oman logged the slick early at around four hundred square kilometres.
Greenpeace's own satellite read put it nearer six hundred, and warned it stood on the verge of an environmental disaster. The official count trailed the oil.
Which matters because —
A spill measured small is a spill fought slowly. In a monsoon week, a downplayed number delays the ships and the booms that actually matter.
[exhales] Bleak. What else moved this week?
Zambia — the president declared re-elected at about sixty per cent, and the loser is heading to court alleging irregularities.

Ukraine put near six hundred drones over the Moscow region overnight; a Russian missile strike killed at least ten near Kharkiv. And Southeast Asia logged seventeen separate disasters in one week — the Flores quake alone settled at sixty-eight dead.
[thoughtful] Three of those four have the same shape as the lead.

They do. A burden landing where the decision was never made — the Omani coast, the Kharkiv street, a flooded valley in Laos. Consequence, this week, kept arriving somewhere other than where it was authored.
Right. The money. The bond market did something dramatic.
[skeptical] The US thirty-year yield hit five point three three per cent. That's the highest since two thousand and seven.
A nineteen-year high. Driven by what?
Fiscal fear, plus oil near ninety-two dollars a barrel. A classic bear steepener — the long end selling off hard.
And then the Treasury blinked. Tell me.
On Wednesday, Secretary Bessent doubled the long-dated buybacks — from two billion dollars to at least four, in the ten-to-thirty-year sector.
[gasps] So the debt manager stepped in between the market and the price of its own debt.

[excited] Exactly. The long end reversed — nine basis points off the thirty, six off the ten. The dollar softened, equities exhaled, and gold pressed a fresh two-month high, around four thousand four hundred dollars.
One fiscal act, rippling through everything.

Rates, then the currency, then metals, then stocks. For a global portfolio: relief for equities, not a green light. A floor under bonds, not a fix. Bitcoin trading as a risk asset, near sixty-four thousand seven hundred.
[wry] And the sceptic's line?

A floor is not a fix. The Treasury's own advisory committee warns buybacks fix liquidity, not the debt profile. If the long end reprices anyway, the reversal is sharper. And this is explanation, not investment advice.
One to watch?
Jackson Hole, next Friday — the new Fed chair's first keynote, eight days after the Treasury eased conditions under him. Watch whether he pushes back, or blesses it.
Closer to home. Singapore.
The haze board lit up again. A dry spell over Sumatra and Kalimantan pushed the watch back on, days before the National Day Rally.
Is it bad yet?
Still moderate. But this season was flagged red back in June — only the second red rating since twenty nineteen. August and September are the peak window.
[thoughtful] And the Rally's this weekend.
Sunday. The Prime Minister's third, and the trailed centrepiece is a major review of family support — the cost of raising children, and caring for ageing parents.
The sceptic there is a gentle one.
A red rating is a probability, not a schedule. A season that fizzles out isn't a false alarm — it's exactly the ending you were hoping for.
Technology. The chips finally crossed the border.
[curious] The first H two hundred boards physically reached China this week — ByteDance and Tencent, about ten thousand each. After a year of paper approvals and rented-cloud workarounds.
So the export controls failed?
Here's the twist — Beijing ordered most of them to stay off the mainland. Parked in Hong Kong, which runs a separate customs regime.
[amused] A city that can't power them at scale.
So they arrive, and they idle. Washington can license the board but not the use; Beijing can take delivery but not concede its own chip policy.
The rule aims at the object. The value's in the access.
That's the sceptic's whole point. Meanwhile the strongest open coder everyone wants — GLM five point three — is still holding its weights back, gated.
So what can I actually run at home tonight, on my own rig?
A new one — Qwen three point eight, twenty-seven billion parameters, dense, and it fits. About twenty-eight gigabytes at eight-bit precision.
[excited] Speed?
Around ninety-eight tokens a second on a single card — which leaves your second card completely free for a draft model and speculative decoding.
But you'd caution me.
[skeptical] The benchmark table is vendor-run and unreproduced. As one reviewer put it — excellent, but it defaults to wildly overthinking things.
The Kit. Headphones.
Bose put its flagship tricks into the cheaper QuietComfort. Three hundred fifty-nine dollars — and, new for this line, wired lossless over USB-C.
Worth it, for a buy-once reader?
It's a value play, not a giant-killer. The cancelling and the comfort are class-leading; the plastic and the bass keep it short of the top. But the wired-lossless is the feature owners point to.
Anything you'd take instead?
[deadpan] For sound-per-dollar, the Sony flagship, at four hundred forty-nine, is the stronger listen — better codecs, less comfortable out of the box. Bose is for the cancelling and the fit.
And the Atelier — buy it once. Today it's watch winders.
And the verdict is the bravest one this desk gives. For a collection like yours — a Grand Seiko among hand-winds — buy none.
[laughs] You've sold me. Why none?
Because a Grand Seiko reaches full reserve in minutes of wear, or a two-minute palm shuffle. A hand-wind gets a winder nothing at all.
But the four-figure ones look incredible.

They're wonderful objects. Also, mostly, objects. Follow the motor and you find the same Japanese Mabuchi assembly — it holds about seventy per cent of the market — inside a thirty-pound box and a four-thousand-dollar one.
[scoffs] So the Swiss price buys everything except a different motor.
Counted rotation, magnetic isolation, sleep phasing, finishing. Not a different heart. Buy one only if a perpetual calendar ever walks into the case.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
Watchmaking. Not collecting — the bench itself. Servicing, regulating, building.
[amused] The only hobby where you break it on purpose. And the gateway moment is universal — the first time a movement ticks back to life in your hands, after you've reassembled it.
Why is it having a moment now?

Because the professionals are leaving. The number of US watch-and-clock repairers fell to one thousand eight hundred eighty in twenty twenty-three, down from two thousand four hundred thirty three years earlier.
[thoughtful] So the amateurs are quietly filling the bench.
The centre of gravity is a single YouTube channel — a man calmly narrating vintage teardowns, now past one point two million subscribers.
And the gear. You said the tools cost more than the watch.
That's the founding joke of the whole hobby. A five-hundred-dollar starter kit, to service a hundred-and-fifty-dollar watch.
Give me the ladder.
Real screwdrivers, good tweezers, a movement holder, and a timegrapher — a Weishi runs about a hundred and forty-five dollars. A full starter bench is around five hundred all in.
Versus the professional tool?
A Witschi is about three thousand. And the forum wisdom is blunt — for most hobbyists, you're never going to notice the difference.
[amused] And the over-the-top tier?

A lathe, and now you're machining your own parts. That's the road from hobbyist to independent watchmaker. The cutting edge is quieter here than most hobbies — full build kits with trilingual video walkthroughs, and Chinese tools now good enough that the old Bergeon-or-nothing orthodoxy is openly questioned.
What does a beginner actually get wrong?
Three things. Pinging a spring across the room. Scratching a bridge with a slipped screwdriver. And over-oiling — the cardinal sin.
[chuckles] I would ping every single spring.
[wry] You would. And the honest sceptic: the real failure mode isn't the ruined movement. It's the fully-kitted bench that does two services and goes quiet. Buying tools is not building skill.
Singapore angle?
A real one. Masterclasses under a Federal master watchmaker, a Watch Academy at a local retailer, and a two-year Patek Philippe apprenticeship, here.
Okay, surface for air. Culture. There is a dinosaur movie.
The End of Oak Street. The It Follows director takes a whole suburban cul-de-sac and drops it into a prehistoric landscape, dinosaur footprint on the front lawn.
[laughs] That is gloriously stupid.
Eighty-five per cent from the critics against seventy-one from the audience — a rare inversion. The reviewers were the enthusiasts, for once.
Family-safe?
A dino-survival adventure with real Spielberg DNA. Your eleven-year-old will happily sit through it.
The Good Life?
Technics dipped the most famous turntable on earth in gold. Twelve thousand numbered units, seven colours.
[skeptical] And the catch is —
It's the same deck as one costing three hundred dollars less. You're paying for the finish and a serial number. Buy it for the object, not the sound.
Family desk. This one matters.
[thoughtful] Organised sport at eleven protects a child's later mental health. But the dose splits by sex — a twenty-three per cent lower risk for boys, only twelve for girls.
[thoughtful] Right as they start dropping out.
About one in three girls quit sport at puberty. And the top reason isn't ability — it's feeling not good enough.
So the evidence-based move is —
Protect any movement she enjoys, right through the exam crunch. Move with her. And don't be alarmist — it's one protective ingredient, not a treatment.
Fitness — quick.
Your VO two max is far more trainable than the calendar suggests. And last month's two-hour strength ceiling now carries a brain number — a twenty-seven per cent lower death rate from dementia.
Two hours of lifting a week. That's the whole game.

Plus your Zone Two cardio. Not a magic bullet — but close to it. One caveat, though — it's observational, self-reported, and it excluded bodyweight work. Train because it works, not because a headline promised a number.
And the Diary. October?
[excited] A wall of stadium nights. The Weeknd, Guns N' Roses, and the Formula One Sprint all colliding in one fortnight. Book your dining first, tickets second.
[excited] And on the plate?
A Ginza omakase just landed at the Capitol Kempinski. And out at Sentosa — a POP Bakery, where for the first time you can actually eat the Labubu.
[warmly] And if you're planning Japan — Kyushu sumo opens in November, tickets drop on the nineteenth of September, and the box seats sell in minutes. Set an alarm.
Noted. The ginkgo avenues too, late November.
[laughs] There's the daughter's headline, right there.
[drawn out] Last thing. The quiet one.
The Undercurrent. Where did we go this time?
[drawn out] Thailand. And the argument is this — Gen Z there hasn't lost its faith. It has cut out the temple.
[curious] Meaning what, exactly?
As the monkhood suffers its worst credibility crisis in a generation — embezzlement, a blackmail scandal, senior monks defrocked — young Thais moved their belief onto TikTok.
How big is this, really?
Three point nine one billion social engagements tied to it in the first eight months of the year. Ninety-four per cent of it on one app.
So what replaced the monk?

A creator with a ring light and an on-screen tip counter. The merit-donation became a twenty-baht livestream. The temple's economics, unbundled into a thousand tiny transactions. A fortune-telling app gathered around half a million users, mostly eighteen to thirty, connected to some seven thousand live readers taking tips of ten to a hundred baht.
[curious] And the brands noticed?
Fast. Marketers coined an ugly word for it — muketing — lucky-colour product drops, blessed-edition packaging. A faith you can test and sell is a faith that's been turned into a product.
Who's pushing back?

[thoughtful] Older, devout Thais — lamenting the commercialisation, warning about the scams. On the same data, about five million of the engagements were negative, and most of those were fraud warnings.
[thoughtful] The temple used to be the platform.
And now the platform is the temple. It's the same arc that took the record label out of music, and the bank out of a payment.
Disintermediation.

And read as an index, it's darker than it sounds. A generation buying control of its luck by the coffee-cup is a generation that feels it controls very little else — the jobs, the politics, the economy.
[warmly] So the thing to watch isn't the luck.
It's the charge they've lost. And that's the whole thread today — the temple, the watchmaker's bench, the export rule, the Treasury. The go-between, quietly routed around.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
